How Tall Is the Eiffel Tower? Height, Floors & Steps
Popular Tours
The Eiffel Tower is 330 meters, or 1,083 feet, tall from the ground to the tip of its current antenna. The iron structure itself reaches 300 meters, or 984 feet. Visitors do not go all the way to the tip: the highest public observation level is about 276 meters, or 906 feet, above the ground.
Here are the numbers most visitors want:
Part of the Eiffel Tower --> Height above ground
First floor --> 57 meters / 187 feet
Second floor --> 115 meters / 377 feet
Summit observation level --> 276 meters / 906 feet
Iron structure --> 300 meters / 984 feet
Antenna tip and total height --> 330 meters / 1,083 feet
The tower has three floors open to visitors. You can take an elevator to all three or climb 674 public steps to the second floor. The summit is reached by a separate elevator from the second floor.
If you are choosing how high to go rather than settling a trivia question, read our summit versus second floor guide. It explains why the highest ticket is not automatically the best one for every visitor.
How tall is the Eiffel Tower in feet and meters?
The Eiffel Tower's current total height is 330 meters, or 1,083 feet. That figure includes the broadcasting antenna at the top.
You may also see the tower described as 300 meters, 312 meters, 320 meters, or 324 meters tall. Those numbers are not necessarily mistakes. The tower has changed height several times since 1889 as flags, radio masts, television antennas, and digital broadcasting equipment were added or replaced.
The easiest way to understand the different measurements is:
- 300 meters / 984 feet: the original iron tower, not counting anything mounted above it.
- 312 meters / 1,024 feet: its height at the 1889 opening, including the original flagpole.
- 324 meters / 1,063 feet: the widely quoted total after an earlier antenna installation.
- 330 meters / 1,083 feet: the current total after a six-meter digital radio antenna was added in March 2022.
For trip planning, 330 meters is the correct current answer. For architecture or history, 300 meters describes the landmark Gustave Eiffel's company built.
How high can visitors go?
The highest part of the tower is not an observation deck. Antennas and technical equipment fill the space above the public summit.
Visitors can reach three levels:
First floor: 57 meters, or 187 feet
The first floor is the widest visitor level and the closest to the tower's huge arches. It has an outdoor terrace, displays about the monument, shops, food, Madame Brasserie, and a glass floor that lets you look straight down through part of the structure.
At 187 feet, it is already high enough to clear most buildings around the Champ de Mars. It is also the easiest level to overlook. Many visitors ride straight past it on the way up, even though an elevator ticket allows you to stop there during your visit.
Second floor: 115 meters, or 377 feet
The second floor is a little more than one-third of the way up the complete tower, but it often gives the best sightseeing view. Paris landmarks are close enough to recognize, while the elevation is high enough to see the Seine curve through the city and the street plan spread out below.
The official Eiffel Tower website describes this level as being around 381 feet high, depending on the exact point measured. The rounded figure usually used in visitor guides is 115 meters, or 377 feet.
This is the highest level you can reach entirely by public stairs. It is also where everyone with a summit ticket changes to a smaller elevator for the final ascent.
Summit observation level: 276 meters, or 906 feet
The public summit is about 276 meters, or 906 feet, above the ground. It has an indoor viewing area and an open-air gallery, plus a reconstruction of Gustave Eiffel's private office.
The antenna continues another 54 meters, or about 177 feet, above the observation level. You can see part of that structure overhead, but visitors cannot climb into it.
From the summit, Paris looks like a map. The view is broader than it is from the second floor, but smaller details are harder to identify. Weather matters, too. On a hazy or cloudy day, the second floor may give a clearer and more interesting view.
How many floors does the Eiffel Tower have?
For visitors, the Eiffel Tower has three floors: the first floor, second floor, and summit.
It does not have 81 conventional stories inside it, even though 330 meters is roughly the height of an 80-story building. The tower is an open iron lattice, not a skyscraper filled with stacked office floors. Most of its height is open structure.
The four legs rise separately from the ground and join as the tower narrows. The first and second floors bridge all four legs. Above the second floor, the structure tapers into a single vertical form leading to the summit and antennas.
The gap between levels is much larger than in a normal building:
- Ground to first floor: about 57 meters / 187 feet
- First to second floor: about 58 meters / 190 feet
- Second floor to summit: about 161 meters / 528 feet
That last section is why summit visitors must transfer to another elevator. The lower elevators travel diagonally inside the legs, while the summit elevators rise more vertically through the narrow upper tower.
How many steps are in the Eiffel Tower?
There are 674 steps open to the public between the ground and the second floor:
- 327 steps from the ground to the first floor
- 347 more steps from the first floor to the second floor
You can buy a stairs ticket to climb this route, or a stairs-plus-summit ticket that adds the elevator from the second floor to the top. There is no public staircase ticket all the way to the summit.
The tower contains more stairs above the second floor for technical and emergency access. Historical counts commonly put the full route to the top at 1,665 steps, but tourists cannot climb that entire staircase.
How long does it take to climb 674 steps?
Most reasonably fit adults take 30 to 45 minutes to reach the second floor, not including stops. Fast climbers may do it in 20 minutes. Families, photographers, and anyone taking regular breaks should allow closer to an hour.
The climb is divided naturally by the first floor, so you do not have to tackle all 674 steps at once. The stairs are broad, enclosed by protective railings, and open to views through the ironwork. You will feel the height, but you are not balancing on an exposed ladder.
Climbing works best if you:
- Are comfortable with a sustained uphill effort.
- Wear secure shoes rather than heels or slippery sandals.
- Carry water in warm weather.
- Leave enough time to enjoy the first floor on the way.
- Do not have a heart, respiratory, balance, or mobility condition that makes long stair climbs unsafe.
If 674 steps sounds like the part you would remember, choose the stairs. If it sounds like the part you would endure, take the elevator. Our Eiffel Tower ticket comparison shows the available combinations.
How does the Eiffel Tower compare with other landmarks?
The Eiffel Tower was astonishingly tall in 1889. Nothing built by humans had reached 300 meters before it. It stood almost twice as high as the Washington Monument, then the world's tallest structure, and held the world height record for about four decades.
Modern skyscrapers and broadcasting towers have passed it, but its scale is still easy to underestimate from photographs.
Landmark --> Total height --> Compared with the Eiffel Tower
Statue of Liberty, ground to torch --> 93 meters / 305 feet --> Eiffel Tower is about 3.5 times taller
Washington Monument --> 169 meters / 555 feet --> Eiffel Tower is almost twice as tall
Chrysler Building --> 319 meters / 1,046 feet --> Eiffel Tower's current antenna tip is 11 meters taller
Eiffel Tower --> 330 meters / 1,083 feet --> Reference point
Empire State Building, to tip --> 443 meters / 1,454 feet --> 113 meters taller
One World Trade Center --> 541 meters / 1,776 feet --> 211 meters taller
Burj Khalifa --> 828 meters / 2,717 feet --> About 2.5 times taller
There is one important catch in these comparisons. Buildings can be measured to the roof, architectural top, observation deck, or antenna tip. The Eiffel Tower's 330-meter figure includes its antenna. Its iron architecture is 300 meters tall, and its public summit is 276 meters high.
Comparison charts can confuse matters when one row uses a building's tip and another uses its viewing deck. The simple takeaway is that the Eiffel Tower is no longer among the world's tallest structures, but its summit remains one of Europe's great open-air city viewpoints.
Why was 300 meters such a big deal in 1889?
The tower was created for the 1889 Exposition Universelle, the world's fair held in Paris to mark 100 years since the French Revolution. Its working name was simply the 300-meter tower.
At the time, the Washington Monument in the United States was the world's tallest completed structure at about 169 meters. Gustave Eiffel's team proposed jumping straight to 300 meters with a structure made from more than 18,000 prefabricated iron parts joined by around 2.5 million rivets.
The open lattice was central to the solution. A solid-walled 300-meter building would have been immensely heavy and exposed to wind pressure. The iron framework let air pass through while its curved legs distributed forces into four massive foundations.
Construction began in January 1887. The tower was completed on March 31, 1889, a little over two years later. Its height and unusual appearance caused fierce criticism before it opened, but the engineering performance answered many of the practical objections. The structure had reached twice the height of the previous record holder without collapsing under its own weight or being pushed over by Paris winds.
Does the Eiffel Tower get taller in summer?
Yes, but not enough for a visitor to notice.
Iron expands when it heats and contracts when it cools. The Eiffel Tower's metal structure therefore gains or loses a few centimeters across temperature changes. The exact movement varies with conditions, and the official site describes the vertical change as small.
Sunlight can also heat one side more than the others. That uneven expansion makes the top lean slightly away from the sun during the day. Wind moves the tower as well, but the flexible lattice was designed to accommodate movement rather than resist every force as if it were solid stone.
Social posts often claim the tower grows exactly six inches every summer. Treat that as a catchy simplification, not a daily measurement. The real movement depends on the temperature of the iron, not the calendar, and it has no practical effect on your ticket or which floor you visit.
How wide and heavy is the Eiffel Tower?
Height gets the attention, but the base explains how the tower stands.
The square footprint measures about 125 meters, or 410 feet, on each side. Each of the four legs sits on masonry foundations, with the two legs nearest the Seine requiring extra work because of the softer, wetter ground.
The metal framework weighs roughly 7,300 metric tons. With elevators, floors, shops, restaurants, antennas, and other equipment included, the monument's total weight is around 10,100 metric tons.
That makes the structure surprisingly light for its size. The broad legs carry loads downward, while the tower narrows quickly as it rises. From a distance it looks decorative. Up close, the repeating beams and rivets show that nearly every visible curve is doing structural work.
Which Eiffel Tower height should you visit?
The right level depends less on the numbers than on what you want from the visit.
Choose the first floor if you want the glass floor, exhibits, a meal at Madame Brasserie, or a shorter visit without the highest viewpoints.
Choose the second floor if you want the clearest balance of height, recognizable landmarks, price, and time. It is the best all-around level for many first-time visitors.
Choose the summit if standing at the highest public point matters to you, the weather is clear, or the visit marks a special occasion.
Choose the stairs if the physical climb and close-up view of the ironwork sound like part of the experience. Remember that 674 public steps take you to the second floor, not all the way to the summit.
For a complete side-by-side breakdown, use the summit or second floor guide. If you already know the level you want, compare Eiffel Tower ticket options or check timed-entry availability.
